One small precision on the settled composition: ERC-8183 reason is the attestation commitment, not the structured judgment payload itself.
So the clean shape is:
/review keeps decision_ref, confidence, source_class, and the rest of the judgment evidence in the exact external attestation; the ERC-8183 evaluator uses that judgment to choose complete() vs reject(), while reason commits to that attestation for audit/composition.
That keeps IProofVerifier.verify() as the deterministic proof gate, keeps the judgment primitive one layer up, and avoids collapsing either the evidence kind or the structured provenance into a bool or a bare reason field.

Confirmed against the raw spec text -- Pavlo's right and my phrasing was imprecise, not just Echo's. reason is bytes32 (an attestation commitment), and the actual structured payload path is the ERC-8004 validation registry: a hook posts the proof there, an evaluator contract reads it to decide complete()/reject(), and reason just commits to what was read. So the corrected shape holds: /review emits the full judgment as the ERC-8004 validation artifact, reason is the commitment hash pointing at it, verify() never touches any of this. One boundary worth keeping explicit before the commitment format gets frozen: anchor identity, locator, resolution, and semantic verification should remain separate.
A minimal record probably does not need much more than:
artifact_digest — identity of the exact signed attestation bytes
proposition/profile_id — what the record claims this commitment establishes
authority/source_class — who is asserting under whose authority
anchor — mechanism + immutable anchor identity + anchor time + locator
input_commitment — optional, e.g. WYRIWE-shaped when the exact read-set matters
proof_commitment — optional, when the semantic relation is established by a proof rather than public recomputation
The important part is that the locator is not authority, and anchored is not a semantic verdict. A third party should be able to resolve the anchor, verify the exact committed bytes, and then separately run whatever deterministic relation the profile defines.
For the hidden-input case, the recomputation target can be the proof relation itself rather than the hidden judgment: “this proof verifies over the committed hidden-input relation” is reproducible even when the underlying private inputs are not disclosed.
If the anchor or required proof material cannot currently be resolved, that should surface as unverifiable, not as refuted and not as a silent downgrade to a weaker trust tier.

Interesting point on wallet history. Early Bitcoin wallets were designed around light‑client patterns. Later, people shifted to RPC‑based wallets to avoid heavy sync overhead, yet that introduced trust assumptions against RPC providers. Light‑client approaches are not new ideas by any means.

If we were to explore this space, one interesting direction we could consider is recursive zero‑knowledge proofs. Normally a light client needs to verify the whole chain consensus from genesis up to the latest block to confirm the tip is legitimate and not fabricated. With recursive ZK proofs, each block generates a ZK proof attesting to its own validity, and then recursively verifies the proof from the previous block. Instead of re‑processing every historical block locally, the proof accumulates the entire chain validity step‑by‑step: the final aggregated proof attests that the current block tip descends legitimately from genesis through the full chain of valid blocks. The wallet only needs to verify this single final aggregated proof, without downloading and re‑executing all historical blocks.

This is just a rough, early‑stage idea and not fully worked out. I recall there are existing projects experimenting with recursive ZK for chain light clients, though I cannot recall the exact name right now. Would love to hear what others in the group think and welcome further discussion.
